entries.title: Methods
error_states: Triple returns a value other than three times its input — run_Triple(x).r != 3*x.
A method changes an in-parameter instead of treating it as read-only — final_x != initial_x.

laws.name: Triple input-output relation
laws.equation: forall x:int, run_Triple(x).r == 3*x; run_Triple(x).r is the final out-parameter
laws.falsifier: exhibit x with run_Triple(x).r != 3*x

laws.name: In-parameter preservation
laws.equation: forall x:int, final_x(run_Triple(x)) == x
laws.falsifier: exhibit x with final_x(run_Triple(x)) != x

entries.breaker_note: Treat even a basic method as an input-output relation and look for an input that violates it.
entries.implementer_note: Trace assignments symbolically and remember that the final values of out-parameters are the returned values.

entries.title: Assert Statements
error_states: A reachable execution arrives at assert r == 3*x + 1 with r == 3*x, so the assertion is false.
A few tested inputs pass, but an untested input reaches a false assertion — sampling is mistaken for proof.

laws.name: Universal assertion safety
laws.equation: forall i, Reaches(i,A) => A(StateAtA(i)); i ranges over all inputs and A is the asserted predicate
laws.falsifier: exhibit input i with Reaches(i,A) && !A(StateAtA(i))

entries.breaker_note: Turn each assertion into a universal property over every input and every execution that reaches it.
entries.implementer_note: Prove assertions symbolically; successful runs on selected inputs do not discharge the obligation.

entries.title: Working with the Verifier
error_states: Triple computes r == 3*x but the specification asserts r == 10*x — the written assertion is wrong except at x == 0.
A failing early assertion filters out bad executions, making a later assertion appear valid even though the method is not globally correct.
A true target condition remains unproved because a required precondition, invariant, lemma, or intermediate assertion is missing.

laws.name: Assertion filtering plus proof obligation
laws.equation: AfterAssert(R,A) == {s | R(s) && A(s)}, while safety requires forall s, R(s) => A(s); R is the reachable-state predicate before assert A
laws.falsifier: exhibit state s with R(s) && !A(s), even if all states in AfterAssert(R,A) satisfy later assertions

entries.breaker_note: A verifier error may expose a code defect, specification defect, or missing proof fact; seek a concrete reachable counterexample before classifying it.
entries.implementer_note: Localize the gap with intermediate assertions, then supply the missing precondition, stronger invariant, lemma, or proof step without confusing surviving traces with correctness.

entries.title: Control Paths
error_states: The then branch establishes r == 3*x but the else branch returns a different value.
Two nondeterministic guards overlap and one enabled branch violates the postcondition, even though another enabled branch succeeds.
A proof uses a branch guard that is false on the execution being analyzed.

laws.name: All enabled branches preserve the goal
laws.equation: forall s,b, Reach(s) && Enabled(b,s) => Post(Step(b,s)); b ranges over every branch the control construct may choose
laws.falsifier: exhibit state s and enabled branch b with Reach(s) && !Post(Step(b,s))

laws.name: Triple branch agreement
laws.equation: forall x,b, EnabledTripleBranch(b,x) => Result(b,x) == 3*x
laws.falsifier: exhibit x and enabled Triple branch b with Result(b,x) != 3*x

entries.breaker_note: Quantify over every enabled branch, including every choice in an overlapping nondeterministic case.
entries.implementer_note: Analyze each branch under its own guard and prove the common assertion independently for every possible path.

entries.title: Method Contracts
error_states: A caller relies on a fact visible in the method body but absent from the postcondition, so an alternative valid implementation breaks the caller.
Triple is called with an odd x although its implementation requires evenness for exact integer division.
Index is underspecified, but a caller assumes two calls with the same input return equal results.
Min returns a value below both inputs but not equal to either input — m <= x && m <= y holds while m is not the minimum.

laws.name: Implementation satisfies its contract
laws.equation: forall x,y, Pre(x) && Returns(M,x,y) => Post(x,y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y with Pre(x) && Returns(M,x,y) && !Post(x,y)

laws.name: Call-site admissibility
laws.equation: forall x, LegalCall(M,x) iff Pre(x)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a call argument x with LegalCall(M,x) && !Pre(x)

laws.name: Opaque-client consequence
laws.equation: Client claim C is justified iff forall y, Post(x,y) => C(x,y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y with Post(x,y) && !C(x,y)

laws.name: Exact minimum specification
laws.equation: MinSpec(x,y,m) iff m <= x && m <= y && (m == x || m == y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y,m with m <= x && m <= y && m != x && m != y

entries.breaker_note: Subsections 1.4.0 and 1.4.1 make underspecification testable: search all outputs allowed by the postcondition, not just the current body’s output.
entries.implementer_note: Prove preconditions at calls and postconditions at returns; strengthen a specification when an allowed but unintended result defeats a client property.

entries.title: Functions
error_states: Two invocations of a function with equal arguments produce different results.
A caller uses a function outside its declared precondition.
A method returns r != 3*x while satisfying the weaker condition Average(r,3*x) == 3*x.
A proof treats a transparent function as an unconstrained result instead of unfolding its body.

laws.name: Function determinism
laws.equation: forall c1,c2, Args(c1) == Args(c2) => Result(c1) == Result(c2); c1 and c2 are invocations of the same function
laws.falsifier: exhibit two invocations c1,c2 with Args(c1) == Args(c2) && Result(c1) != Result(c2)

laws.name: Transparent definition
laws.equation: forall a, f(a) == Body_f(a); Body_f is the function body with formal parameters replaced by a
laws.falsifier: exhibit argument a with f(a) != Body_f(a)

laws.name: Function-call admissibility
laws.equation: forall a, LegalUse(f,a) iff Pre_f(a)
laws.falsifier: exhibit argument a with LegalUse(f,a) && !Pre_f(a)

laws.name: Exact Triple result
laws.equation: forall x, TriplePrime(x) == 3*x
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,r with Average(r,3*x) == 3*x && r != 3*x

entries.breaker_note: Demand determinism and unfold transparent definitions; also test whether a function-based specification admits unintended values.
entries.implementer_note: Use the function body as an equation, establish its precondition at every use, and strengthen weak result specifications to the intended relation.

entries.title: Compiled versus Ghost
error_states: A compiled result depends on a ghost variable, so erasing ghost state changes the observable output.
A compiled computation calls a ghost method for a value that will not exist at run time.
Ghost assertions or proof computations survive erasure and alter executable behavior or effects.

laws.name: Ghost noninterference
laws.equation: forall c,g1,g2, CompiledOut(P,c,g1) == CompiledOut(P,c,g2); c is compiled state and g1,g2 are ghost states
laws.falsifier: exhibit c,g1,g2 with CompiledOut(P,c,g1) != CompiledOut(P,c,g2)

laws.name: Erasure preservation
laws.equation: CompiledObs(P,input) == CompiledObs(EraseGhost(P),input)
laws.falsifier: exhibit input with CompiledObs(P,input) != CompiledObs(EraseGhost(P),input)

entries.breaker_note: Subsection 1.6.0 motivates an erasure test: vary or remove all ghost material and compare compiled observations.
entries.implementer_note: Keep proof-only values flowing only into ghost constructs so compilation can erase them without changing executable results.

entries.title: Program State
error_states: A state at a program point omits an in-scope variable or assigns a value to a variable that is out of scope.
MyMethod starts from x == 37 but reaches a state other than x == 37, y == 56, a == 40, b == 16 at program point 9.
A correctness argument includes an initial state such as x == 2 even though the precondition requires 10 <= x.

laws.name: State-domain equals scope
laws.equation: dom(StateAt(p)) == Scope(p); dom gives the variables valued by the state at program point p
laws.falsifier: exhibit program point p and variable v with v in exactly one of dom(StateAt(p)) and Scope(p)

laws.name: MyMethod contract over states
laws.equation: forall s0,sf, s0.x >= 10 && RunMyMethod(s0,sf) => sf.y >= 25
laws.falsifier: exhibit initial state s0 and final state sf with s0.x >= 10 && RunMyMethod(s0,sf) && sf.y < 25

entries.breaker_note: Phrase defects as valuations at named program points and restrict initial valuations with the precondition.
entries.implementer_note: Represent predicates as sets of states, track scope changes, and reason over all initial states denoted by the precondition.

entries.title: Floyd Logic
error_states: An annotation before a statement holds, but executing the statement reaches a state that violates the next annotation.
The method precondition does not imply the first body annotation.
The final body annotation holds but is too weak to imply the method postcondition.

laws.name: Decorated-edge preservation
laws.equation: forall s,s', A_p(s) && Step(p,q,s,s') => A_q(s'); A_p and A_q annotate adjacent program points
laws.falsifier: exhibit adjacent points p,q and states s,s' with A_p(s) && Step(p,q,s,s') && !A_q(s')

laws.name: Boundary implications
laws.equation: forall s, Pre(s) => A_entry(s), and forall s, A_exit(s) => Post(s)
laws.falsifier: exhibit state s with Pre(s) && !A_entry(s), or A_exit(s) && !Post(s)

entries.breaker_note: Attack every local transition and both method boundaries; one failed implication refutes the decorated proof.
entries.implementer_note: Derive annotations forward from reachable states or backward from the goal, then check every adjacent transition and boundary implication.

entries.title: Hoare Triples
error_states: A state satisfies P, but S terminates in a state that does not satisfy Q.
A state satisfies P, but S crashes before producing a Q-state.
A state satisfies P, but S diverges instead of terminating.

laws.name: Total-correctness Hoare triple
laws.equation: Valid({P} S {Q}) iff forall s, P(s) => TerminatesWithoutCrash(S,s) && Q(Final(S,s))
laws.falsifier: exhibit state s with P(s) and either Crash(S,s), Diverge(S,s), or !Q(Final(S,s))

entries.breaker_note: A Hoare-triple red test is one initial P-state witnessing a crash, divergence, or final violation of Q.
entries.implementer_note: Discharge both functional correctness and total correctness; reaching Q only on successful executions is insufficient.

entries.title: Strongest Postconditions and Weakest Preconditions
error_states: Assignment reasoning substitutes the new x into itself incorrectly and accepts a state outside the true weakest precondition.
A swap loses an old value because the proof lacks logical variables for the initial x and y.
A simultaneous assignment is analyzed as two sequential assignments, so a right-hand side reads an already-updated variable.
An uninitialized local is assumed to have a convenient value instead of an arbitrary value of its type.
A backward proof weakens an intermediate assertion, so the earlier annotation no longer implies the required condition.

laws.name: Assignment weakest precondition
laws.equation: WP[x := E,Q] == Q[x := E]; substitution replaces post-state x by pre-state expression E
laws.falsifier: exhibit pre-state s with CandidateWP(s) != Q[x := E](s)

laws.name: Simultaneous-assignment substitution
laws.equation: WP[x,y := E,F,Q] == Q[x,y := E,F], with E and F both evaluated in the pre-state
laws.falsifier: exhibit pre-state where sequential substitution and simultaneous substitution give different truth values

laws.name: Arbitrary local introduction
laws.equation: WP[var x,Q] == forall x, Q
laws.falsifier: exhibit a candidate pre-state accepted even though some initial value of x falsifies Q

laws.name: Assignment strongest postcondition
laws.equation: SP[x := E,P] == exists x0, P[x := x0] && x == E[x := x0]; x0 denotes the overwritten value
laws.falsifier: exhibit post-state included by a candidate SP with no old value x0 satisfying the equation

laws.name: Swap relation
laws.equation: forall X,Y, RunSwap(X,Y) == (Y,X)
laws.falsifier: exhibit X,Y with RunSwap(X,Y) != (Y,X)

entries.breaker_note: Subsections 2.3.0-2.3.4 supply the main attacks: preserve old values, distinguish simultaneous from sequential updates, and quantify uninitialized locals universally.
entries.implementer_note: Work backward by substitution, simplify as you go, and only strengthen backward annotations; use fresh logical variables or existential old values when updates overwrite information.

entries.title: WP and SP
error_states: A transformer computes WP forward or SP backward, reversing the dependency order.
A simultaneous assignment uses lists of mismatched lengths or non-simultaneous substitution.
Local-variable introduction uses existential quantification in WP or universal quantification in SP.

laws.name: Assignment transformer pair
laws.equation: WP[x := E,Q] == Q[x := E] and SP[x := E,P] == exists x0, P[x := x0] && x == E[x := x0]; x,E,x0 may be equal-length lists
laws.falsifier: exhibit assignment and predicate for which either computed transformer differs from the stated predicate

laws.name: Local-introduction transformer pair
laws.equation: WP[var x,Q] == forall x, Q and SP[var x,P] == exists x, P
laws.falsifier: exhibit predicate where a candidate transformer uses the opposite quantifier and changes the truth value

entries.breaker_note: Instantiate the transformer equations from Subsections 2.4.0-2.4.1 and compare predicates extensionally.
entries.implementer_note: For goals, compute WP backward; for reachable facts, compute SP forward, preserving simultaneous list substitution and the correct quantifiers.

entries.title: Conditional Control Flow
error_states: The proof checks only the then branch and accepts a state whose else execution violates the goal.
The strongest postcondition conjoins branch results, losing states reachable through exactly one branch.
A branch is analyzed without conjoining or assuming its guard.
A nested conditional is simplified as though an infeasible inner branch were feasible.

laws.name: Conditional strongest postcondition
laws.equation: SP[if B {S} else {T},P] == SP[S,P && B] || SP[T,P && !B]
laws.falsifier: exhibit a post-state reachable through one guarded branch that a candidate SP excludes, or an unreachable state it includes

laws.name: Conditional weakest precondition
laws.equation: WP[if B {S} else {T},Q] == (B => WP[S,Q]) && (!B => WP[T,Q])
laws.falsifier: exhibit pre-state s accepted by a candidate WP where the branch selected by B fails Q

entries.breaker_note: Subsection 2.5.0 gives the red-test equations: split by the guard and demand correctness of whichever branch is selected.
entries.implementer_note: Conjoin guards when moving forward, assume guards when moving backward, disjoin branch SP results, and conjoin guarded WP obligations.

entries.title: Sequential Composition
error_states: WP for S;T is computed in source order, so T's requirement is not propagated backward through S.
SP for S;T applies T before S, reversing the actual execution order.
Two sequential assignments are treated as one simultaneous assignment and therefore read different values.

laws.name: Sequential SP composition
laws.equation: SP[S;T,P] == SP[T,SP[S,P]]
laws.falsifier: exhibit P,S,T and post-state where a candidate SP differs from SP[T,SP[S,P]]

laws.name: Sequential WP composition
laws.equation: WP[S;T,Q] == WP[S,WP[T,Q]]
laws.falsifier: exhibit P,S,T,Q and pre-state accepted by a candidate WP but rejected by WP[S,WP[T,Q]], or conversely

entries.breaker_note: Use order-sensitive programs to distinguish sequential composition from reversal or simultaneous execution.
entries.implementer_note: Push reachable facts through S then T, but pull a desired postcondition through T then S.

entries.title: Method Calls and Postconditions
error_states: A caller proves a property by inspecting the current method body although the postcondition permits another implementation that violates it.
Formal and actual parameter names capture one another because the call semantics does not use fresh names.
An underspecified output is treated existentially, so the proof chooses one favorable result instead of covering every result allowed by the postcondition.

laws.name: Assumption transformers
laws.equation: WP[assume E,Q] == (E => Q) and SP[assume E,P] == P && E
laws.falsifier: exhibit state where a candidate assume transformer has a different truth value

laws.name: Opaque-call weakest precondition
laws.equation: WP[t := M(E),Q] == forall y', R[x,y := E,y'] => Q[t := y']; R is M's postcondition and y' is fresh
laws.falsifier: exhibit E,Q,y' with R[x,y := E,y'] && !Q[t := y'] although the candidate precondition accepts the call

entries.breaker_note: Subsections 2.7.0-2.7.2 require fresh renaming and universal quantification over every result admitted by the postcondition.
entries.implementer_note: Desugar a call into fresh parameters, actual-input assignment, postcondition assumption, and output assignment; never use the opaque body at the call site.

entries.title: Assert Statements
error_states: An assertion is treated as an assumption, so E is used without proving that it holds.
An SP-only argument declares assert E safe because it describes only crash-free executions and omits the crash obligation.
A method postcondition is assumed at calls even though no proof establishes it for the method body.

laws.name: Assert weakest precondition
laws.equation: WP[assert E,Q] == E && Q
laws.falsifier: exhibit state s with Q(s) && !E(s) that a candidate precondition accepts

laws.name: Assume weakest precondition
laws.equation: WP[assume E,Q] == E => Q
laws.falsifier: exhibit state s where a candidate assume precondition differs from E(s) => Q(s)

laws.name: SP cannot distinguish assert from assume
laws.equation: SP[assert E,P] == SP[assume E,P] == P && E
laws.falsifier: exhibit P,E and post-state where either SP differs from P && E

laws.name: Discharge call assumptions
laws.equation: forall M, Pre_M => WP[Body_M,Post_M]
laws.falsifier: exhibit method M and input satisfying Pre_M but not WP[Body_M,Post_M]

entries.breaker_note: Subsection 2.8.0 shows why crash-freedom tests must use WP rather than SP alone; Subsection 2.8.2 requires every assumed callee postcondition to be proved at its implementation.
entries.implementer_note: Conjoin assertion conditions into backward obligations, while using assumptions only where another verified component supplies the fact.

entries.title: Weakest Liberal Preconditions
error_states: WLP is used alone, so an execution that crashes at assert false is ignored and the program is declared correct.
A proof assumes WP == WLP even though the statement may crash.
A proposed SP/WLP pair violates the Galois connection or its distribution laws.
WP is treated as an upper adjoint satisfying WP[S,true] == true, which fails for assert false.

laws.name: Conservative-precondition decomposition
laws.equation: WP[S,Q] == WLP[S,Q] && WP[S,true]
laws.falsifier: exhibit S,Q,state s where the two sides have different truth values

laws.name: SP-WLP Galois connection
laws.equation: Valid(SP[S,P] => Q) iff Valid(P => WLP[S,Q])
laws.falsifier: exhibit S,P,Q for which exactly one implication is valid

laws.name: Adjoint distribution
laws.equation: SP[S,OR_i(P_i)] == OR_i(SP[S,P_i]) and WLP[S,AND_i(Q_i)] == AND_i(WLP[S,Q_i])
laws.falsifier: exhibit S and a predicate family for which either distribution equality fails

laws.name: Empty-family identities
laws.equation: SP[S,false] == false and WLP[S,true] == true
laws.falsifier: exhibit S and state accepted by SP[S,false], or rejected by WLP[S,true]

laws.name: WP is not the WLP upper adjoint
laws.equation: WP[assert false,true] == false
laws.falsifier: exhibit a state accepted by a candidate WP for assert false with postcondition true

entries.breaker_note: Subsections 2.9.0-2.9.2 separate postcondition reasoning from crash freedom and provide adjunction and distribution checks for semantic transformers.
entries.implementer_note: When using WLP, conjoin the independent no-crash obligation WP[S,true]; do not transfer WLP's upper-adjoint identities to WP.

entries.title: Method Calls with Preconditions
error_states: A caller invokes M(E) with P(E) false.
A caller assumes the postcondition R(E,y') even when the precondition was never established.
The proof checks Q for one allowed output instead of every y' satisfying R(E,y').
A non-fresh formal name captures a caller variable and changes the substituted precondition or postcondition.

laws.name: Complete call weakest precondition
laws.equation: WP[t := M(E),Q] == P[x := E] && forall y', R[x,y := E,y'] => Q[t := y']; P and R are the callee precondition and postcondition
laws.falsifier: exhibit E and state where P[x := E] is false, or exhibit y' with R[x,y := E,y'] && !Q[t := y'], while a candidate precondition accepts

laws.name: Fresh-input precondition equivalence
laws.equation: WP[x' := E; assert P[x := x'],Q] == WP[assert P[x := E],Q], when x' is fresh and absent from E and Q
laws.falsifier: exhibit E,P,Q and fresh x' for which the two weakest preconditions differ

entries.breaker_note: Attack both conjuncts of the call equation: illegal actual inputs and allowed outputs that defeat the caller's continuation.
entries.implementer_note: Use the Subsection 2.10 desugaring: fresh parameters, assign actual inputs, assert the precondition, assume the postcondition, then assign actual outputs.

entries.title: Function Calls
error_states: A proof treats transparent Abs as an arbitrary result and cannot establish its non-negativity.
Abs returns a negative result on some input because its conditional definition is unfolded or implemented incorrectly.
A conditional expression is simplified using only one branch, producing a false result for inputs selecting the other branch.

laws.name: Transparent function unfolding
laws.equation: f(E) == Body_f[x := E]; Body_f is the defining expression of f
laws.falsifier: exhibit function f and argument E with f(E) != Body_f[x := E]

laws.name: Absolute-value definition
laws.equation: Abs(x) == (if x < 0 then -x else x) and forall x, Abs(x) >= 0
laws.falsifier: exhibit x with Abs(x) != (if x < 0 then -x else x), or Abs(x) < 0

laws.name: Abs assertion discharge
laws.equation: WP[assert 0 <= Abs(E),Q] == Q for integer expression E
laws.falsifier: exhibit integer E and state where the computed weakest precondition differs from Q

entries.breaker_note: Use the function body itself as the oracle and split conditional expressions over both guards.
entries.implementer_note: Unfold transparent definitions, distribute surrounding operators across the conditional, and simplify each guarded branch.

entries.title: Partial Expressions
error_states: Division evaluates with denominator zero.
An array access uses i < 0 or i >= a.Length.
MinusOne(y) is called with y <= 0, violating its function precondition.
A short-circuit operator evaluates or demands definedness of a right operand that its left operand makes unreachable.
An if-then-else expression demands definedness of the unselected branch or fails to demand it for the selected branch.

laws.name: Assignment definedness
laws.equation: WP[x := E,Q] == Defined(E) && Q[x := E]
laws.falsifier: exhibit state s with !Defined(E)(s) that a candidate weakest precondition accepts

laws.name: Primitive domain guards
laws.equation: Defined(c/d) iff d != 0; Defined(a[i]) iff 0 <= i < a.Length; Defined(MinusOne(y)) iff y > 0
laws.falsifier: exhibit a zero denominator, out-of-range index, or nonpositive MinusOne argument that is classified as defined

laws.name: Short-circuit definedness
laws.equation: Defined(E && F) == Defined(E) && (E => Defined(F)); Defined(E || F) == Defined(E) && (E || Defined(F)); Defined(E => F) == Defined(E) && (E => Defined(F))
laws.falsifier: exhibit E,F where a candidate rule requires F on a short-circuited path or omits it on an evaluated path

laws.name: Conditional-expression definedness
laws.equation: Defined(if B then E else F) == Defined(B) && (if B then Defined(E) else Defined(F))
laws.falsifier: exhibit B,E,F where the selected branch is undefined but the expression is accepted, or only the unselected branch is undefined and it is rejected

entries.breaker_note: Convert every partial operation into an explicit assertion and test short-circuit and branch-sensitive definedness separately.
entries.implementer_note: Precede partial operations conceptually with their domain obligations, then propagate those obligations through WP using evaluation order.

entries.title: Method Correctness
error_states: The method precondition holds for an input, but the body fails to establish the postcondition.
The body establishes the postcondition only for a subset of legal inputs.
The body reaches a correct-looking result on normal runs but can crash or diverge from a state satisfying the precondition.

laws.name: Method implementation correctness
laws.equation: forall s, P(s) => WP[Body,Q](s); P is the method precondition and Q its postcondition
laws.falsifier: exhibit state s with P(s) && !WP[Body,Q](s)

entries.breaker_note: The tight refutation is a legal initial state outside the body's weakest precondition for the promised result.
entries.implementer_note: Compute WP of the complete body against the postcondition, including crash and termination obligations, then prove the declared precondition implies it.

entries.title: Notes: Law of the Excluded Miracle
error_states: Executable statement semantics claims to guarantee the impossible postcondition false from a real initial state.
An implementation inserts assume false and uses the resulting absence of executions as proof of arbitrary behavior.

laws.name: Law of the Excluded Miracle
laws.equation: forall executable statements S, WP[S,false] == false
laws.falsifier: exhibit executable statement S and state s with WP[S,false](s)

laws.name: Assume is a partial specification command
laws.equation: WP[assume false,false] == true
laws.falsifier: exhibit a state where WP[assume false,false] evaluates to false

entries.breaker_note: Reject miraculous executable implementations; the Notes explicitly identify assume as a specification-level partial command that violates the executable law.
entries.implementer_note: Keep assumption constructs in the reasoning layer and ensure executable code cannot establish correctness merely by eliminating all executions.

entries.title: The Endless Problem
error_states: BadDouble recurses forever, so its ensures clause is never realized by a returned result.
PartialId called with odd x recurses with the same x, so the call stack grows without bound although y == x would hold if it returned.
Squarish can keep changing guess forever, so x*x == y is not guaranteed to be reached.
Impossible makes an immediate self-call with no base case, so no result can satisfy its postcondition.
Admitting Dubious makes a == 1 + a and therefore proves 0 == 1, making the logic inconsistent.

laws.name: total correctness combines value correctness and termination
laws.equation: TotalCorrect(S,Q) = PartialCorrect(S,Q) && Terminates(S) (S = program; Q = postcondition)
laws.falsifier: exhibit S,Q with PartialCorrect(S,Q) = true and Terminates(S) = false

laws.name: recursive definitions must not imply arithmetic contradiction
laws.equation: Dubious() = 1 + Dubious() => 0 = 1 (Dubious() = recursive integer function result)
laws.falsifier: exhibit an admitted function f with f() = 1 + f()

entries.breaker_note: Reject any implementation that satisfies its postcondition only conditionally on termination, and reject recursive definitions that make false assertions derivable.
entries.implementer_note: Prove total correctness: establish the postcondition and supply a well-founded decrease for every recursive path before treating the result as meaningful.

entries.title: Avoiding Infinite Recursion
error_states: A recursive call keeps the same or increases its termination metric, so the verifier cannot rule out infinite recursion.
Using -lo as a metric permits an unbounded descending chain outside the nonnegative integers, so decrease alone does not establish termination.
SeqSum uses a metric that does not decrease when lo advances, leaving its recursive call unjustified.

laws.name: every recursive call strictly decreases a nonnegative metric
laws.equation: forall call c -> d: mu(c) >= 0 && mu(d) < mu(c) (mu = decreases expression; c,d = caller and callee activations; < = termination-order decrease)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a recursive call c -> d with mu(c) < 0 or mu(d) >= mu(c)

laws.name: SeqSum interval distance decreases
laws.equation: hi - (lo + 1) < hi - lo (lo,hi = SeqSum bounds; lo < hi)
laws.falsifier: exhibit lo,hi with lo < hi but hi - (lo + 1) >= hi - lo

entries.breaker_note: Make every recursive edge expose a strictly smaller nonnegative metric; specifically test the interval-distance decrease used by SeqSum.
entries.implementer_note: Choose a progress measure that counts remaining work, such as hi - lo, and check the caller-to-callee obligation on every branch.

entries.title: Well-Founded Relations
data_structures: bool, int, real, set<T>, seq<T>, and inductive-datatype values
error_states: A proposed reduction relation relates a value to itself, allowing a self-recursive call to appear decreasing.
A proposed relation is nontransitive, so two locally decreasing calls do not compose into a valid descent argument.
A real-valued order based on ordinary strict less-than admits an infinite descending sequence such as 1, 1/2, 1/3, ... .
An integer metric is treated as decreasing below a negative caller value, even though Dafny's integer reduction relation requires a nonnegative caller.

laws.name: well-founded reduction is irreflexive
laws.equation: not (a >_wf a) (a = any metric value; >_wf = chosen well-founded reduction relation)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a with a >_wf a

laws.name: well-founded reduction is transitive
laws.equation: (a >_wf b && b >_wf c) => a >_wf c (a,b,c = metric values)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a,b,c with a >_wf b && b >_wf c && not (a >_wf c)

laws.name: well-founded reduction has no infinite descending chain
laws.equation: not exists a[0],a[1],... such that forall i >= 0, a[i] >_wf a[i+1] (a[i] = metric values)
laws.falsifier: exhibit an infinite sequence a[0],a[1],... with a[i] >_wf a[i+1] for every i

laws.name: Dafny integer reduction
laws.equation: X >_wf y iff (y < X && 0 <= X) (X,y = int metrics; >_wf = Dafny's integer reduction relation)
laws.falsifier: exhibit X,y:int for which exactly one of X >_wf y and (y < X && 0 <= X) holds

entries.breaker_note: Test the chosen metric relation itself for irreflexivity, transitivity, and absence of infinite descent before testing program-specific decreases clauses.
entries.implementer_note: Use Dafny's built-in well-founded order for the metric type and remember that an integer caller must be nonnegative; arbitrary real strict descent is not sufficient.

entries.title: Lexicographic Tuples
error_states: A checker accepts a transition from (2,100) to (3,0) because a later component decreased even though the earlier component increased.
A checker rejects a valid proper-prefix descent, such as StudyPlan's one-component metric to Learn's two-component metric.
ExpLess1 and ExpLess2 recurse with the same n, so decreases n alone cannot prove the call from ExpLess1(n) to ExpLess2(n).

laws.name: lexicographic comparison prioritizes earlier components
laws.equation: (a,b) >_lex (a2,b2) iff a >_wf a2 || (a = a2 && b >_wf b2) (a,b,a2,b2 = tuple components; >_lex = lexicographic reduction; >_wf = component reduction)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a,a2,b,b2 with not (a >_wf a2) && b >_wf b2 && (a,b) >_lex (a2,b2)

laws.name: a proper prefix reduces to the longer tuple
laws.equation: properPrefix(p,q) => p >_lex q (p,q = bounded tuples; >_lex = lexicographic reduction)
laws.falsifier: exhibit p,q with properPrefix(p,q) && not (p >_lex q)

laws.name: function rank breaks equal-argument mutual recursion
laws.equation: (n,1) >_lex (n,0) && (n,0) >_lex (n - 1,1) for n >= 1 (n = shared argument; tuple = decreases metric)
laws.falsifier: exhibit n >= 1 with not ((n,1) >_lex (n,0)) or not ((n,0) >_lex (n - 1,1))

entries.breaker_note: Apply the tuple laws across Sections 3.3.0–3.3.3: remaining school work, Ackermann, mutual recursion, and the ExpLess refactoring.
entries.implementer_note: Put the dominant progress measure first, use the proper-prefix rule when crossing outer and inner computations, and add a constant rank when mutually recursive functions pass equal arguments.

entries.title: Default decreases in Dafny
error_states: SeqSum relies on the default tuple (s,lo,hi), but its recursive call increases lo rather than decreasing that tuple, so termination is unproved.
StudyPlan relies on the default metric n, but Learn can call StudyPlan(n + 1), so the guessed metric does not descend.
An explicit metric is removed without checking the verifier's new guess, leaving a recursive edge whose guessed metric is not smaller.

laws.name: a default metric is valid only when every call decreases it
laws.equation: Verified(f) => forall call c -> d: default_mu(c) >_wf default_mu(d) (Verified = termination check succeeds; default_mu = verifier's guessed decreases metric)
laws.falsifier: exhibit f and call c -> d with default_mu(c) <=_wf default_mu(d)

laws.name: nondefault progress measures must be stated explicitly
laws.equation: SeqSum_mu(s,lo,hi) = hi - lo && StudyPlan_mu(n) = 40 - n (s = sequence; lo,hi = bounds; n = completed-course count)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a SeqSum call where the default tuple fails to reduce even though hi - lo decreases, or a StudyPlan call where n fails to reduce even though 40 - n decreases

entries.breaker_note: Break any implementation that treats a verifier guess as a theorem when the signature tuple does not represent remaining work.
entries.implementer_note: Inspect the default metric, retain it only when every recursive edge decreases, and write an explicit clause such as hi - lo or 40 - n when the signature order is wrong.

entries.title: Summary
data_structures: recursive and mutually recursive call graphs
error_states: A decreases list is interpreted as unrelated component checks rather than one lexicographic metric, so a valid dominant-component descent is rejected or an invalid later-component descent is accepted.
A recursive branch has no strict decrease in the chosen well-founded order, so the program can continue forever despite correct local result equations.

laws.name: a decreases list denotes one lexicographic tuple
laws.equation: decreases E1,...,Ek = tuple(E1,...,Ek) under >_lex (Ei = listed expressions; >_lex = lexicographic order)
laws.falsifier: exhibit two recursive calls whose acceptance differs between tuple lexicographic comparison and independent component comparison

laws.name: every recursive edge descends
laws.equation: forall recursive calls c -> d: mu(c) >_lex mu(d) (mu = decreases tuple; >_lex = fixed well-founded lexicographic order)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a recursive call c -> d with not (mu(c) >_lex mu(d))

entries.breaker_note: Use the summary as the global gate: a recursive implementation is acceptable only when its decreases tuple descends on every edge.
entries.implementer_note: Expose the metric as a lexicographic tuple and prove each branch's caller-to-callee comparison; omit explicit clauses only when the default guess passes that test.

entries.title: Blue-Yellow Trees
error_states: A value outside BlueLeaf, YellowLeaf, or Node is accepted as a BYTree.
Node is constructed with the wrong arity or with a child that is not itself a BYTree.
Code assumes every BYTree is a leaf and mishandles a legal Node value.

laws.name: BYTree values are exhausted by their constructors
laws.equation: t in BYTree => (t = BlueLeaf || t = YellowLeaf || exists l,r: t = Node(l,r)) (t = any BYTree value; l,r = BYTree subtrees)
laws.falsifier: exhibit t in BYTree with t != BlueLeaf && t != YellowLeaf && not (exists l,r: t = Node(l,r))

entries.breaker_note: Use the datatype declaration as an exhaustive shape contract for every tree value and constructor use.
entries.implementer_note: Define the three variants first, then handle each constructor explicitly; treat the recursive Node parameters as BYTree values.

entries.title: Matching on Datatypes
error_states: A match on BYTree omits a legal variant such as YellowLeaf, so a valid input has no defined branch.
BlueCount returns the wrong result for a leaf because BlueLeaf and YellowLeaf branches are confused.
BlueCount(Node(left,right)) counts only one subtree or binds the child patterns incorrectly, so blue leaves are lost.

laws.name: BlueCount follows all BYTree constructors
laws.equation: BlueCount(BlueLeaf) = 1 && BlueCount(YellowLeaf) = 0 && BlueCount(Node(l,r)) = BlueCount(l) + BlueCount(r) (BlueCount = blue-leaf count; l,r = subtrees)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a BYTree t with BlueCount(t) != the corresponding constructor equation

laws.name: match cases are exhaustive for the source datatype
laws.equation: covered(match,BYTree) = {BlueLeaf,YellowLeaf,Node} (covered = constructor cases supplied by match)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a BYTree match with covered(match,BYTree) missing one of BlueLeaf, YellowLeaf, or Node

entries.breaker_note: Turn each constructor branch into a red case and include the recursive sum law for Node.
entries.implementer_note: Write an exhaustive match, bind each constructor parameter in scope, and reduce recursive branches to the corresponding subtrees.

entries.title: Discriminators and Destructors
error_states: The Node discriminator reports true for a leaf or false for a Node.
A destructor such as t.left is evaluated on a leaf, violating its Node precondition.
A destructor returns the wrong child, so Node(l,r).left or Node(l,r).right is not the original subtree.

laws.name: the discriminator agrees with the constructor variant
laws.equation: IsNode(t) = t.Node? (IsNode = predicate defined by a match; Node? = built-in Node discriminator)
laws.falsifier: exhibit t with IsNode(t) != t.Node?

laws.name: destructors recover Node parameters
laws.equation: t = Node(l,r) => t.Node? && t.left = l && t.right = r (l,r = original subtrees; left,right = destructors)
laws.falsifier: exhibit l,r with Node(l,r).left != l or Node(l,r).right != r

laws.name: destructor definedness is its discriminator precondition
laws.equation: defined(t.left) = t.Node? (defined = the destructor precondition holds)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a leaf t with defined(t.left) = true

entries.breaker_note: Check both the variant test and the guarded field projection; a destructor must never be used outside its constructor case.
entries.implementer_note: Use a match or discriminator before accessing a destructor, and let the discriminator/destructor equations recover the original Node children.

entries.title: Structural Inclusion
error_states: A recursive tree function calls itself on a value that is not a structurally included child, so termination cannot be established.
A recursive call chain cycles through equal or larger datatype values, so the function can recurse forever.

laws.name: constructor children are structurally smaller
laws.equation: Node(t,u) >_wf t && Node(t,u) >_wf u (>_wf = structural-inclusion reduction; t,u = BYTree values)
laws.falsifier: exhibit t,u with not (Node(t,u) >_wf t) or not (Node(t,u) >_wf u)

laws.name: structural inclusion has no infinite descent
laws.equation: not exists a[0],a[1],... such that forall i >= 0, a[i] >_wf a[i+1] (a[i] = inductive-datatype values; >_wf = structural inclusion)
laws.falsifier: exhibit an infinite sequence of inductive-datatype values with a[i] >_wf a[i+1] for every i

entries.breaker_note: Require every recursive call on a datatype to move to an actual constructor parameter, not merely to a value that looks smaller.
entries.implementer_note: Use the datatype argument as the decreases value; pattern matching exposes the structurally included children and Dafny can discharge the decrease.

entries.title: Enumerations
error_states: A color outside Blue, Yellow, Green, or Red is accepted as a Color.
IsSwedishFlagColor classifies Green or Red as Swedish-flag colors, or rejects Blue or Yellow.
IsLithuanianFlagColor accepts Blue or rejects a non-Blue color.

laws.name: Color is an exhaustive finite enumeration
laws.equation: c in Color iff (c = Blue || c = Yellow || c = Green || c = Red) (c = color value)
laws.falsifier: exhibit c in Color with c != Blue && c != Yellow && c != Green && c != Red

laws.name: Swedish flag colors are exactly blue and yellow
laws.equation: IsSwedishFlagColor(c) = (c = Blue || c = Yellow) (c = Color value)
laws.falsifier: exhibit c with IsSwedishFlagColor(c) != (c = Blue || c = Yellow)

laws.name: Lithuanian flag colors are every non-blue color
laws.equation: IsLithuanianFlagColor(c) = (c != Blue) (c = Color value)
laws.falsifier: exhibit c with IsLithuanianFlagColor(c) != (c != Blue)

entries.breaker_note: Use the finite constructor set to test both enum exhaustiveness and color predicates.
entries.implementer_note: Represent each color as a parameterless constructor and dispatch predicates directly from the finite set of variants.

entries.title: Type Parameters
error_states: Tree<int> accepts a Leaf carrying a string or another payload of the wrong type.
Size returns a value other than 1 for a leaf or drops one subtree at a Node.
AllBlue accepts a non-blue Color leaf or returns true when either child subtree is not all blue.

laws.name: generic Tree preserves its payload type
laws.equation: Tree<T> = Leaf(T) | Node(Tree<T>,Tree<T>) (T = payload type; | = constructor alternatives)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a value v with v in Tree<T> and v = Leaf(x) where x is not of type T

laws.name: Size counts one leaf and both subtrees
laws.equation: Size(Leaf(x)) = 1 && Size(Node(l,r)) = Size(l) + Size(r) (x = payload; l,r = Tree<T> subtrees)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,l,r with Size(Leaf(x)) != 1 or Size(Node(l,r)) != Size(l) + Size(r)

laws.name: AllBlue is structural over Tree<Color>
laws.equation: AllBlue(Leaf(c)) = (c = Blue) && AllBlue(Node(l,r)) = (AllBlue(l) && AllBlue(r)) (c = Color payload; l,r = Tree<Color> subtrees)
laws.falsifier: exhibit c,l,r with either AllBlue(Leaf(c)) != (c = Blue) or AllBlue(Node(l,r)) != (AllBlue(l) && AllBlue(r))

entries.breaker_note: Test the generic shape independently of the payload type, then test recursive functions for preserving every leaf and subtree.
entries.implementer_note: Parameterize both the datatype and reusable functions by T; pattern-match Leaf and Node and make recursive results combine over both children.

entries.title: Abstract Syntax Trees for Expressions
error_states: Eval dispatches a legal Const, Var, or Node expression to the wrong case or drops a Node's argument list.
Eval returns a nonzero value for an unmapped variable even though the specified default is zero.
EvalList uses the wrong identity for an empty Add or Mul list, or combines the head and tail with the wrong operation.
EvalList or Eval makes a recursive call on a non-structurally-smaller expression or list, allowing nontermination.

laws.name: literal evaluation is identity
laws.equation: Eval(Const(c),env) = c (c = literal nat; env = map<string,nat>)
laws.falsifier: exhibit c,env with Eval(Const(c),env) != c

laws.name: missing variables evaluate to zero
laws.equation: Eval(Var(s),env) = if s in env.Keys then env[s] else 0 (s = variable name; env = environment map)
laws.falsifier: exhibit s,env with s not in env.Keys and Eval(Var(s),env) != 0

laws.name: Node evaluation delegates to its argument list
laws.equation: Eval(Node(op,args),env) = EvalList(args,op,env) (op = Add or Mul; args = List<Expr>)
laws.falsifier: exhibit op,args,env with Eval(Node(op,args),env) != EvalList(args,op,env)

laws.name: list evaluation uses operation identities and combines head with tail
laws.equation: EvalList(Nil,Add,env) = 0 && EvalList(Nil,Mul,env) = 1 && EvalList(Cons(e,tail),op,env) = combine(op,Eval(e,env),EvalList(tail,op,env)) (combine(Add,x,y) = x + y; combine(Mul,x,y) = x * y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit e,tail,op,env with any listed EvalList equation false

laws.name: mutual recursion follows structural inclusion
laws.equation: Node(op,args) >_wf args && Cons(e,tail) >_wf e && Cons(e,tail) >_wf tail (>_wf = structural-inclusion reduction)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a recursive call whose caller and callee arguments do not satisfy one of these structural reductions

entries.breaker_note: Use the evaluator equations and structural decreases together: Sections 4.6's AST, list, operation, and environment cases are one mutually recursive contract.
entries.implementer_note: Pattern-match Expr and List, use zero and one as the Add and Mul identities, combine head and tail under the selected operation, and rely on structural arguments for termination.

entries.title: Summary
error_states: Two constructor applications with different payloads compare equal, so the payload cannot be recovered by deconstruction.
A value with no declared constructor variant is admitted, so a supposedly exhaustive match can miss an input.
A recursive proof treats a child as no smaller than its constructor-built parent, so structural termination is lost.
An infinite or cyclic datatype value is admitted, defeating the finite-structure basis of induction and termination.

laws.name: constructors are injective
laws.equation: C(x1,...,xk) = C(y1,...,yk) => x1 = y1 && ... && xk = yk (C = any datatype constructor; xi,yi = constructor parameters)
laws.falsifier: exhibit C,x1,...,xk,y1,...,yk with C(x1,...,xk) = C(y1,...,yk) and some xi != yi

laws.name: distinct constructors form distinct variants
laws.equation: C(...) != D(...) for C != D (C,D = distinct datatype constructors)
laws.falsifier: exhibit distinct constructors C,D and arguments with C(...) = D(...)

laws.name: inductive structure is finite and well-founded
laws.equation: C(...,x,...) >_wf x && not exists a[0],a[1],... with forall i >= 0, a[i] >_wf a[i+1] (>_wf = structural inclusion)
laws.falsifier: exhibit a constructor value and child where not (C(...,x,...) >_wf x), or an infinite structural-descending chain

entries.breaker_note: Use constructor injectivity, variant separation, and finite structural descent as the chapter-wide datatype laws.
entries.implementer_note: Define values bottom-up, deconstruct only declared variants, and prove recursive datatype functions by reducing to structurally included parameters.

entries.title: Declaring a Lemma
error_states: the lemma specifies only x <= More(x), so an implementation returning More(x) == x satisfies the contract despite violating the intended strict growth
the postcondition mentions the wrong argument, such as x < More(x + 1), so callers learn nothing about More(x)
an intended input restriction is omitted from requires, so callers apply the lemma where its intended antecedent is false

laws.name: Increasing
laws.equation: forall x:int. x < More(x)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x:int with More(x) <= x

laws.name: Lemma contract soundness
laws.equation: forall x. Pre(x) => Post(x), where Pre and Post are the declared precondition and postcondition; Pre(x)=true when no precondition is declared
laws.falsifier: exhibit x with Pre(x) && !Post(x)

entries.breaker_note: Treat the lemma declaration as the public law: make the domain explicit and state strict growth rather than a weaker approximation.
entries.implementer_note: Represent the property as a ghost method whose requires clause controls applicability and whose ensures clause states exactly what callers may assume.

entries.title: Using a Lemma
error_states: the code invokes Increasing(a) but not Increasing(More(a)), so the final two-step-growth assertion lacks its middle link
the code invokes Increasing on c == More(More(a)) instead of on b == More(a), proving a fact about the next value rather than the value used by the assertion
Increasing(More(a)) is called only when a < 1000, but 2 <= More(More(a)) - a is asserted after the branches rejoin
a lemma is instantiated with a value that differs from the expression occurring at the failing assertion

laws.name: Two-step strict growth
laws.equation: forall a:int. More(More(a)) >= a + 2
laws.falsifier: exhibit a:int with More(More(a)) < a + 2

laws.name: All-path instance coverage
laws.equation: forall a,p. ReachFinal(p,a) => Have_p(a < More(a)) && Have_p(More(a) < More(More(a))), where Have_p(P) means P was established on path p
laws.falsifier: exhibit a and a path p reaching the final assertion with either growth fact missing

entries.breaker_note: Test the composed behavior, and require the two lemma instances on every path reaching the assertion; a true lemma called on the wrong value is irrelevant.
entries.implementer_note: Instantiate postconditions on the exact intermediate values used by the consumer. Lemma knowledge is path-sensitive even though lemma calls do not mutate state.

entries.title: Proving a Lemma
error_states: a body-less lemma is treated as an axiom, allowing callers to assume strict growth without any proof
the proof handles x <= 0 but leaves the positive branch without the induction hypothesis, so the postcondition is not established on every return path
the recursive proof calls Increasing(x), making no progress and attempting to justify the goal by an infinite circular call
the proof recurses on x + 2 or another non-decreasing argument, so its termination argument is invalid

laws.name: More defining equation
laws.equation: forall x:int. More(x) = (if x <= 0 then 1 else More(x - 2) + 3)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x:int with More(x) != (if x <= 0 then 1 else More(x - 2) + 3)

laws.name: Increasing theorem
laws.equation: forall x:int. x < More(x)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x:int with More(x) <= x

laws.name: Induction descent
laws.equation: forall x:int. x > 0 => proofArg(x) = x - 2 && proofArg(x) < x, where proofArg is the argument of the recursive lemma call
laws.falsifier: exhibit x:int with x > 0 and proofArg(x) >= x

entries.breaker_note: Reject an unproved declaration as evidence and target both the theorem and the recursive proof's progress measure.
entries.implementer_note: Split on the same condition as More, discharge the base case by unfolding, and obtain the positive case from Increasing(x - 2). The decreasing recursive call is the induction argument.

entries.title: Back to Basics
error_states: a proof assertion is false at a reachable program point even though earlier assertions were true
the positive branch unfolds More but omits Increasing(x - 2), leaving no fact that bounds More(x - 2)
two consecutive formulas are written down even though the first does not imply the second
a previously established formula is omitted as redundant even though a variable occurring in it changed
one branch establishes x < More(x), but the other reaches the join without establishing the postcondition

laws.name: Reachable assertion validity
laws.equation: forall proof points p and states s. Reach(p,s) => A_p(s), where A_p is the assertion at p
laws.falsifier: exhibit a reachable pair (p,s) with !A_p(s)

laws.name: Base-case implication
laws.equation: forall x:int. x <= 0 && More(x) = 1 => x < More(x)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x:int with x <= 0 && More(x) = 1 && More(x) <= x

laws.name: Inductive-step implication
laws.equation: forall x:int. x > 0 && More(x) = More(x - 2) + 3 && x - 2 < More(x - 2) => x < More(x)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x:int satisfying the three premises with More(x) <= x

entries.breaker_note: Section 5.3.0 turns the proof into local implications; Section 5.3.1 makes each implication independently checkable as an assertion. Ask for a reachable counterexample at the first invalid step.
entries.implementer_note: Lay out precondition, branch facts, unfolding equations, induction hypothesis, and postcondition as a Floyd-logic chain. Remove assertions only after confirming their facts remain available and their variables are unchanged.

entries.title: Proof Calculations
error_states: a calc step uses == where only <= holds, silently strengthening an inequality into a false equality
the step 3*x + 2*n <= 3*x + 3*n is used for an arbitrary integer n; it fails when n is negative
successive comparison operators point in incompatible directions, so their endpoint relation does not follow by transitivity
a checked hint calls a lemma on the wrong arguments and therefore does not establish the relation between its adjacent expressions

laws.name: Checked calc step
laws.equation: forall steps i. R_i(e_i,e_(i+1)) holds after executing hint_i, where e_i and e_(i+1) are adjacent expressions and R_i is the displayed operator
laws.falsifier: exhibit a step i and inputs with hint_i satisfied but !R_i(e_i,e_(i+1))

laws.name: Compatible-chain endpoint
laws.equation: Compatible(R_0,...,R_(n-1)) && all i. R_i(e_i,e_(i+1)) => Chain(e_0,e_n), where Compatible means the operators compose in one direction and Chain is their transitive endpoint relation
laws.falsifier: exhibit a calculation whose displayed steps hold but whose claimed endpoint relation fails

laws.name: Nonnegative arithmetic bound
laws.equation: forall x:int,n:nat. 3*x + n + n <= 3*(x + n)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x:int,n:nat with 3*x + n + n > 3*(x + n)

entries.breaker_note: Make every displayed transformation separately falsifiable, including its domain assumptions and relation direction. Section 5.4.0 requires hints to prove the adjacent step rather than merely state something true.
entries.implementer_note: Start from the more structured side, choose ==, <=, >=, or implication according to the information actually available, and put required lemma calls inside the corresponding checked hint.

entries.title: Example: Reduce
error_states: Reduce returns a value greater than x, violating the upper bound despite its recursive subtraction
Reduce returns exactly x - 2*m, satisfying the stated non-strict lower bound but violating the stronger strict bound established by the calculation
the proof replaces 2*(m/2) by m for odd m, using a false integer-division equality
the recursive call keeps m unchanged or increases it, so the reduction and its inductive proof may not terminate
the recursive case increments x or subtracts m incorrectly, violating the defining recurrence

laws.name: Reduce defining equation
laws.equation: forall m:nat,x:int. Reduce(m,x) = (if m = 0 then x else Reduce(floor(m/2),x + 1) - m)
laws.falsifier: exhibit m:nat,x:int with Reduce(m,x) != (if m = 0 then x else Reduce(floor(m/2),x + 1) - m)

laws.name: Reduce bounds
laws.equation: forall m:nat,x:int. x - 2*m < Reduce(m,x) && Reduce(m,x) <= x
laws.falsifier: exhibit m:nat,x:int with Reduce(m,x) <= x - 2*m || Reduce(m,x) > x

laws.name: Halving arithmetic and descent
laws.equation: forall m:nat. 2*floor(m/2) = m - (m % 2) && 2*floor(m/2) <= m && (m > 0 => floor(m/2) < m)
laws.falsifier: exhibit m:nat where a halving equality or inequality fails, or m > 0 with floor(m/2) >= m

entries.breaker_note: Sections 5.5.0 and 5.5.1 supply a two-sided oracle for Reduce; odd m is the sharp counterexample class for the tempting but false doubling-after-halving equality.
entries.implementer_note: Split on m = 0, unfold Reduce, invoke the bound on floor(m/2), and continue with an inequality rather than equality. Use floor(m/2) < m as the induction discharge.

entries.title: Example: Commutativity of Multiplication
error_states: repeated-addition multiplication depends on argument order, yielding Mult(x,y) != Mult(y,x)
the x = 0 case returns a nonzero result because recursion in y is mishandled
the proof calls MultCommutative(y - 1,x - 1) under decreases (x,y) when y - 1 can exceed x, so the recursive call is not lexicographically smaller
a recursive call subtracts 1 from a natural argument without first establishing that the argument is positive

laws.name: Repeated-addition definition
laws.equation: forall x,y:nat. Mult(x,y) = (if y = 0 then 0 else x + Mult(x,y - 1))
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y:nat with Mult(x,y) != (if y = 0 then 0 else x + Mult(x,y - 1))

laws.name: Multiplication commutativity
laws.equation: forall x,y:nat. Mult(x,y) = Mult(y,x)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y:nat with Mult(x,y) != Mult(y,x)

laws.name: Lexicographic proof descent
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y:nat and one listed branch condition whose recursive argument is not lexicographically smaller than (x,y)

entries.breaker_note: Test commutativity asymmetrically, especially at zero and with x far smaller than y, and audit every proposed induction call against the declared ordering.
entries.implementer_note: Partition the input space into cases that make each recursive call legal. When swapping decremented arguments would break the default ordering, call the symmetric lemma instance whose first component actually decreases.

entries.title: Example: Mirroring a Tree
data_structures: binary trees Tree<T> with Leaf and Node constructors
error_states: Mirror swaps only the root children and leaves descendants unmirrored; a shallow double swap may pass involution while the Node defining equation fails
Mirror changes a leaf payload instead of returning the same leaf
Mirror drops or duplicates a subtree, so applying it twice does not reconstruct the original tree
Mirror loses or duplicates leaves, so Size(Mirror(t)) differs from Size(t)

laws.name: Structural mirror equations
laws.equation: forall d,l,r. Mirror(Leaf(d)) = Leaf(d) && Mirror(Node(l,r)) = Node(Mirror(r),Mirror(l))
laws.falsifier: exhibit a payload d or subtrees l,r for which either constructor equation fails

laws.name: Mirror involution
laws.equation: forall t:Tree<T>. Mirror(Mirror(t)) = t
laws.falsifier: exhibit t:Tree<T> with Mirror(Mirror(t)) != t

laws.name: Leaf-count preservation
laws.equation: forall t:Tree<T>. Size(Mirror(t)) = Size(t), where Size(Leaf(d))=1 and Size(Node(l,r))=Size(l)+Size(r)
laws.falsifier: exhibit t:Tree<T> with Size(Mirror(t)) != Size(t)

entries.breaker_note: Sections 5.7.0 and 5.7.1 give independent structural, involution, and leaf-count checks; retain the structural equation because involution alone admits unintended transformations.
entries.implementer_note: Match on the tree constructor, unfold until recursive subtrees are exposed, invoke the induction hypothesis on both subtrees, then rebuild the target. Section 5.7.2 warns that a valid intermediate equality is not necessarily the stated goal.

entries.title: Example: Working on Abstract Syntax Trees
data_structures: expression ASTs Expr with Const, Var, and Node constructors
finite maps from strings to natural numbers used as environments
error_states: Substitute replaces the wrong variable name or misses a nested occurrence, so evaluation no longer agrees with updating the environment
SubstituteList handles the head but skips the tail, so substitution correctness fails for a later list element
Unit(Mul) is defined as 0 or Unit(Add) as 1, causing optimization to remove a non-unit expression and change evaluation
Shorten returns the wrong constant for an empty argument list or mishandles a singleton list, changing the Node's value
OptimizeAndFilter drops a non-unit optimized argument, so Optimize changes the expression's value under some environment

laws.name: Substitution semantics
laws.equation: forall e,n,c,env. Eval(Substitute(e,n,c),env) = Eval(e,update(env,n,c)), where update(env,n,c) maps n to c and agrees with env elsewhere
laws.falsifier: exhibit e,n,c,env with Eval(Substitute(e,n,c),env) != Eval(e,update(env,n,c))

laws.name: List substitution semantics
laws.equation: forall args,op,n,c,env. EvalList(SubstituteList(args,n,c),op,env) = EvalList(args,op,update(env,n,c))
laws.falsifier: exhibit args,op,n,c,env where the two EvalList results differ

laws.name: Operator units
laws.equation: Unit(Add) = 0 && Unit(Mul) = 1
laws.falsifier: exhibit op in {Add,Mul} with Unit(op) different from its stated value

laws.name: Shorten semantic equivalence
laws.equation: forall op,args,env. Eval(Shorten(op,args),env) = Eval(Node(op,args),env)
laws.falsifier: exhibit op,args,env with Eval(Shorten(op,args),env) != Eval(Node(op,args),env)

laws.name: Optimize-and-filter semantic equivalence
laws.equation: forall args,op,env. Eval(Node(op,OptimizeAndFilter(args,Unit(op))),env) = Eval(Node(op,args),env)
laws.falsifier: exhibit args,op,env where optimizing and filtering the arguments changes the Node evaluation

laws.name: Optimization semantic preservation
laws.equation: forall e,env. Eval(Optimize(e),env) = Eval(e,env)
laws.falsifier: exhibit e,env with Eval(Optimize(e),env) != Eval(e,env)

entries.breaker_note: Section 5.8.0 requires substitution tests across every AST constructor and list position. Section 5.8.1 requires semantic equivalence for Add and Mul, with empty, singleton, unit-containing, and nested argument lists.
entries.implementer_note: Mirror the mutually recursive evaluators and transformations with mutually recursive lemmas. Prove the Shorten and OptimizeAndFilter helper contracts, then compose them in OptimizeCorrect; structure each proof by the same constructor cases as its function.

entries.title: List Definition
error_states: A constructor admits mixed element types — `Cons(true, Cons(3, Nil))` is accepted as a `List`.
A `Nil` is treated as a `Cons`, so `head(Nil)` or `tail(Nil)` is read instead of being rejected.
A `Cons(x,xs)` exposes the wrong head or tail — `head(Cons(x,xs)) != x` or `tail(Cons(x,xs)) != xs`.

laws.name: List constructor coverage
laws.equation: For every v:List<T>, isNil(v) == true || isCons(v) == true
laws.falsifier: exhibit v:List<T> with isNil(v) == false and isCons(v) == false

laws.name: Cons destructor laws
laws.equation: head(Cons(x,xs)) == x && tail(Cons(x,xs)) == xs
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,xs with head(Cons(x,xs)) != x or tail(Cons(x,xs)) != xs

laws.name: Homogeneous list typing
laws.equation: type(Cons(x,xs)) == List<T> iff type(x) == T && type(xs) == List<T>
laws.falsifier: exhibit x=true,y=3 with Cons(x,Cons(y,Nil)) accepted as one typed List

entries.breaker_note: Check that every list has exactly the Nil-or-Cons shape, destructors expose the constructor fields, and element types remain homogeneous.
entries.implementer_note: Represent lists with only Nil and Cons, pattern-match before destructing, and preserve one element type T throughout.

entries.title: Length
error_states: The empty list is miscounted — `Length(Nil) != 0`.
A nonempty list loses the head from its count — `Length(Cons(x,xs)) != 1 + Length(xs)`.
Appending an element with `Snoc` does not increase length by one — `Length(Snoc(xs,x)) != Length(xs) + 1`.

laws.name: Empty length
laws.equation: Length(Nil) == 0
laws.falsifier: exhibit the empty list with Length(Nil) != 0

laws.name: Cons length recursion
laws.equation: Length(Cons(x,xs)) == 1 + Length(xs)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,xs with Length(Cons(x,xs)) != 1 + Length(xs)

laws.name: Snoc length
laws.equation: Length(Snoc(xs,x)) == Length(xs) + 1
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,x with Length(Snoc(xs,x)) != Length(xs) + 1

entries.breaker_note: Use the zero-case and one-step recursion equations as the basic count oracle for every list operation.
entries.implementer_note: Match on the list; return zero for Nil and one plus the recursive tail length for Cons, then discharge Snoc by induction.

entries.title: Intrinsic versus Extrinsic Specifications
error_states: Append drops or duplicates elements — `Length(Append(xs,ys)) != Length(xs) + Length(ys)`.
Appending `Nil` changes a list — `Append(xs,Nil) != xs` or `Append(Nil,xs) != xs`.
Grouping concatenations changes the result — `Append(Append(xs,ys),zs) != Append(xs,Append(ys,zs))`.
Snoc is not append of a singleton — `Snoc(xs,x) != Append(xs,Cons(x,Nil))`.

laws.name: Append length
laws.equation: For xs,ys:List<T>, Length(Append(xs,ys)) == Length(xs) + Length(ys)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,ys with Length(Append(xs,ys)) != Length(xs) + Length(ys)

laws.name: Append units
laws.equation: Append(Nil,xs) == xs && Append(xs,Nil) == xs
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs with either Append(Nil,xs) != xs or Append(xs,Nil) != xs

laws.name: Append associativity
laws.equation: Append(Append(xs,ys),zs) == Append(xs,Append(ys,zs))
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,ys,zs with the two parenthesizations unequal

laws.name: Snoc as singleton append
laws.equation: Snoc(xs,x) == Append(xs,Cons(x,Nil))
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,x with Snoc(xs,x) != Append(xs,Cons(x,Nil))

entries.breaker_note: Use the unit and associativity laws from subsection 6.2.0, together with length and the Snoc singleton law, to detect malformed concatenation.
entries.implementer_note: Make universally useful facts such as Append length intrinsic; prove multi-call algebraic facts extrinsically by induction, especially the first-list argument, as advised in subsection 6.2.0.

entries.title: Take and Drop
error_states: A strict Take or Drop call is accepted with `n > Length(xs)`, so the body reaches `head` or `tail` on a Nil value.
Take returns a non-prefix or the wrong prefix — `Take(xs,n)` is not the first n elements of xs.
Drop returns a non-suffix or the wrong suffix — `Drop(xs,n)` does not start after the first n elements.
Splitting and recombining loses or reorders data — `Append(Take(xs,n),Drop(xs,n)) != xs`.

laws.name: Strict domain
laws.equation: defined(Take(xs,n)) && defined(Drop(xs,n)) => n <= Length(xs)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs=Nil,n=1 with a strict Take or Drop call accepted

laws.name: Take-drop recombination
laws.equation: n <= Length(xs) => Append(Take(xs,n),Drop(xs,n)) == xs
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,n with n <= Length(xs) and recombination unequal to xs

laws.name: Take-drop over append
laws.equation: Take(Append(xs,ys),Length(xs)) == xs && Drop(Append(xs,ys),Length(xs)) == ys
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,ys where either extracted part differs

entries.breaker_note: Test the strict precondition and the split/recombine laws; these expose both off-by-one errors and element loss.
entries.implementer_note: Use the precondition to justify `head` and `tail`, recurse on `n-1`, and prove recombination by induction; the liberal variants must agree whenever `n <= Length(xs)`.

entries.title: At
error_states: At accepts an improper index — `At(xs,Length(xs))` is defined or reads from Nil.
At returns the wrong element at a valid index — `At(xs,i) != the element after i predecessors`.
Dropping a valid index produces Nil or a wrong head — `Drop(xs,i).Cons?` is false or `head(Drop(xs,i)) != At(xs,i)`.
At over Append chooses the wrong list or uses the wrong offset.

laws.name: At domain
laws.equation: defined(At(xs,i)) => i < Length(xs)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,i with i >= Length(xs) and At(xs,i) accepted

laws.name: At after Drop
laws.equation: i < Length(xs) => Drop(xs,i).Cons? && At(xs,i) == head(Drop(xs,i))
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,i with i < Length(xs) and either conjunct false

laws.name: At over Append
laws.equation: i < Length(Append(xs,ys)) => At(Append(xs,ys),i) == if i < Length(xs) then At(xs,i) else At(ys,i-Length(xs))
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,ys,i in range where the selected value or offset is wrong

entries.breaker_note: Treat proper indexing and the At/Drop/Append correspondence as one contract: every At call must have a proven index and correct branch offset.
entries.implementer_note: Carry length facts into the recursive call; establish `Drop(xs,i).Cons?` before reading its head, and split AtAppend at `Length(xs)`.

entries.title: Find
error_states: Find returns a position outside the list — `Find(xs,y) > Length(xs)`.
Find returns a later occurrence instead of the first — `Find(Cons(y,Cons(y,Nil)),y) != 0`.
Find reports a hit at an index whose element is not y — `Find(xs,y) < Length(xs)` but `At(xs,Find(xs,y)) != y`.
An earlier position already contains y — `i < Find(xs,y)` but `At(xs,i) == y`.
Appending or dropping a prefix gives the wrong absolute index.

laws.name: Find range
laws.equation: 0 <= Find(xs,y) && Find(xs,y) <= Length(xs)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,y with Find(xs,y) < 0 or Find(xs,y) > Length(xs)

laws.name: Find hit-or-absence
laws.equation: Find(xs,y) == Length(xs) || At(xs,Find(xs,y)) == y
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,y with Find(xs,y) < Length(xs) and At(xs,Find(xs,y)) != y

laws.name: First occurrence
laws.equation: i < Find(xs,y) => At(xs,i) != y
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,y,i with i < Find(xs,y) and At(xs,i) == y

laws.name: Find over Append
laws.equation: Find(xs,y) == Length(xs) || Find(Append(xs,ys),y) == Find(xs,y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,ys,y with y present in xs and the appended search index changed

laws.name: Find after Drop
laws.equation: i <= Find(xs,y) => Find(xs,y) == Find(Drop(xs,i),y) + i
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,y,i satisfying the premise with unequal absolute indices

entries.breaker_note: The red tests should distinguish first hit, absence sentinel, and index translation across Append and Drop.
entries.implementer_note: Match on the head first, recurse only after proving the equality-characteristic is available, and use the range contract to justify every At call.

entries.title: List Reversal
error_states: Reverse changes the multiset or order of elements — it is not the mathematical reverse of the input.
ReverseAux loses or duplicates the accumulator — its result is not the reversed input followed by acc.
The efficient Reverse disagrees with the reference SlowReverse.
Reversing an Append uses the wrong order, or Reverse is not an involution.

laws.name: Reverse preserves length
laws.equation: Length(Reverse(xs)) == Length(xs)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs with unequal input and output lengths

laws.name: Reference correctness
laws.equation: Reverse(xs) == SlowReverse(xs)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs where the efficient and slow reversals differ

laws.name: Accumulator correctness
laws.equation: ReverseAux(xs,acc) == Append(Reverse(xs),acc)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,acc where ReverseAux(xs,acc) differs from reversed xs followed by acc

laws.name: Reverse of Append
laws.equation: Reverse(Append(xs,ys)) == Append(Reverse(ys),Reverse(xs))
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,ys violating the reversed concatenation order

laws.name: Reverse involution
laws.equation: Reverse(Reverse(xs)) == xs
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs with Reverse(Reverse(xs)) != xs

entries.breaker_note: Use the reference implementation, accumulator equation, length, reverse-of-Append, and involution as mutually reinforcing witnesses against loss or order errors.
entries.implementer_note: Introduce the accumulator invariant `ReverseAux(xs,acc) == Append(reverse(xs),acc)`; in the Cons case normalize with SnocAppend and Append associativity before applying the induction hypothesis.

entries.title: Lemmas in Expressions
error_states: A proof-authoring statement changes the expression's result — `value(S;E) != value(E)`.
An At call is accepted without proving its index proper, for example `Length(xs)-1-i >= Length(Reverse(xs))`.
ReverseAux returns a value that violates its intrinsic postcondition after the Cons branch.
Mutual recursion between ReverseAux and ReverseAuxHelper fails to decrease, permitting an infinite call chain.
AtReverse is stated with an undefined At expression because the reversed-list length fact is unavailable.

laws.name: Proof-expression erasure
laws.equation: For verified proof statement S and expression E, value(S;E) == value(E)
laws.falsifier: exhibit verified S,E with value(S;E) != value(E)

laws.name: Intrinsic ReverseAux contract
laws.equation: ReverseAux(xs,acc) == Append(SlowReverse(xs),acc)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,acc for which the function result violates its postcondition

laws.name: AtReverse well-definedness
laws.equation: i < Length(xs) => Length(xs)-1-i < Length(Reverse(xs))
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,i satisfying i < Length(xs) but the reversed index is out of range

laws.name: AtReverse symmetry
laws.equation: i < Length(xs) => At(xs,i) == At(Reverse(xs),Length(xs)-1-i)
laws.falsifier: exhibit xs,i in range with unequal mirrored elements

laws.name: Helper decreases
laws.equation: lexrank(tail,Cons(x,acc),0) < lexrank(Cons(x,tail),acc)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,tail,acc where the helper call's Dafny decreases tuple is not smaller

entries.breaker_note: Check that proof statements are semantically erased, every expression precondition is discharged, and the AtReverse symmetry is backed by a valid reversed index.
entries.implementer_note: Place assertions, calculations, or lemma calls before the expression they justify; subsection 6.7.0 supplies the intrinsic-helper pattern, while 6.7.1 supplies the repeated LengthReverse and case-split move.

entries.title: Eliding Type Arguments
error_states: An elided `List` is instantiated with a type other than the enclosing type parameter, so a generic call accepts or returns the wrong element type.
T is elided from a signature even though it appears only in the result, so `At` loses its result type and admits incompatible clients.
Explicit and elided signatures expose different type parameters, so a call type-checks in one form but not the other.

laws.name: Enclosing-parameter List elision
laws.equation: Inside a declaration with enclosing type parameter T, List == List<T> and List<T> == List<T>
laws.falsifier: exhibit a generic declaration where elided List is inferred as a type other than List<T>

laws.name: Signature-preserving elision
laws.equation: Length<T>(xs:List<T>):nat == Length(xs:List):nat
laws.falsifier: exhibit a call accepted by one Length signature but rejected or differently typed by the other

laws.name: Result-type parameter cannot be elided
laws.equation: resultType(At<T>(xs:List<T>,i:nat):T) == T, so T remains explicit
laws.falsifier: exhibit T1 != T2 where an elided At signature gives both List<T1> and List<T2> the same result type

entries.breaker_note: Treat elision as a typing equivalence, not a change in the generic interface; especially preserve T when it appears in At's result.
entries.implementer_note: Use elided List and type parameters only when the enclosing declaration determines them; retain explicit T for result types, as in At.

entries.title: Basic Definitions
error_states: UnaryToNat miscounts a successor — `UnaryToNat(Suc(x)) != 1 + UnaryToNat(x)`.
NatToUnary maps a positive natural to Zero or to the wrong successor chain.
The two conversions are not inverses — `UnaryToNat(NatToUnary(n)) != n` or `NatToUnary(UnaryToNat(x)) != x`.

laws.name: UnaryToNat constructors
laws.equation: UnaryToNat(Zero) == 0 && UnaryToNat(Suc(x)) == 1 + UnaryToNat(x)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x with either constructor equation false

laws.name: NatToUnary constructors
laws.equation: NatToUnary(0) == Zero && NatToUnary(n+1) == Suc(NatToUnary(n)) for n:nat
laws.falsifier: exhibit n:nat where either constructor equation false

laws.name: Unary-to-nat round trip
laws.equation: UnaryToNat(NatToUnary(n)) == n
laws.falsifier: exhibit n:nat with a changed round trip

laws.name: Nat-to-unary round trip
laws.equation: NatToUnary(UnaryToNat(x)) == x
laws.falsifier: exhibit x:Unary with a changed round trip

entries.breaker_note: Use both conversion directions as a finite, structural oracle for the Zero/Suc representation and its arithmetic meaning.
entries.implementer_note: Define each conversion by its constructor cases and prove the two round trips by induction; do not make later Unary proofs depend on conversion alone.

entries.title: Comparisons
error_states: Less accepts Zero as the right operand — `Less(x,Zero) == true`.
Less is reflexive or off by one — `Less(x,x) == true` or `Less(Suc(x),x) == true`.
The relation is nontransitive — `Less(x,y) && Less(y,z)` holds while `Less(x,z)` does not.
Less fails trichotomy, or Below is not total and antisymmetric.

laws.name: Structural Less definition
laws.equation: Less(x,y) == (y != Zero && (x.Suc? ==> Less(x.pred,y.pred)))
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y where the predicate differs from its Zero/Suc definition

laws.name: Less correctness
laws.equation: Less(x,y) <==> UnaryToNat(x) < UnaryToNat(y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y where Less and the natural-number comparison disagree

laws.name: Less transitivity
laws.equation: Less(x,y) && Less(y,z) ==> Less(x,z)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y,z satisfying the two premises but not the conclusion

laws.name: Less trichotomy
laws.equation: exactly_one(Less(x,y), x == y, Less(y,x))
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y with none or more than one of the three propositions true

laws.name: Below total order
laws.equation: Below(x,y) == (Less(x,y) || x == y), with Below(x,y) || Below(y,x) and (Below(x,y) && Below(y,x) ==> x == y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y violating totality or antisymmetry

entries.breaker_note: Break the comparison at Zero/Suc boundaries, then test natural correspondence, transitivity, trichotomy, and the derived total order.
entries.implementer_note: Prove transitivity by assuming its antecedent, splitting on `x.Suc?`, and recursing on predecessors; the implication form supports both forward and reverse use.

entries.title: Addition and Subtraction
error_states: Add miscounts successors — `UnaryToNat(Add(x,y)) != UnaryToNat(x) + UnaryToNat(y)`.
Addition depends on operand order or parenthesization.
Suc or Zero fails to act as the stated successor or unit.
Sub accepts `x < y`, or valid subtraction fails to reconstruct the minuend — `Add(Sub(x,y),y) != x`.

laws.name: Add correctness
laws.equation: UnaryToNat(Add(x,y)) == UnaryToNat(x) + UnaryToNat(y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y where the Unary and nat sums disagree

laws.name: Add units
laws.equation: Add(x,Zero) == x && Add(Zero,x) == x
laws.falsifier: exhibit x violating either unit equation

laws.name: Suc distribution
laws.equation: Suc(Add(x,y)) == Add(Suc(x),y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y violating successor distribution

laws.name: Add associativity
laws.equation: Add(Add(x,y),z) == Add(x,Add(y,z))
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y,z with unequal parenthesizations

laws.name: Add commutativity
laws.equation: Add(x,y) == Add(y,x)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y with unequal operand order results

laws.name: Sub correctness
laws.equation: !Less(x,y) => UnaryToNat(Sub(x,y)) == UnaryToNat(x) - UnaryToNat(y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y satisfying !Less(x,y) with an incorrect difference

laws.name: Add after Sub
laws.equation: !Less(x,y) => Add(Sub(x,y),y) == x
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y satisfying !Less(x,y) with failed reconstruction

entries.breaker_note: Use correspondence plus unit, successor, associativity, commutativity, and valid-subtraction reconstruction to catch arithmetic and boundary defects.
entries.implementer_note: Follow the definition's chosen induction parameter; prove the opposite-sided unit/distribution laws as helper lemmas, and guard Sub with `!Less(x,y)`.

entries.title: Multiplication
error_states: Multiplication by Zero is not Zero — `Mul(Zero,y) != Zero`.
The successor case does not add one copy of y — `Mul(Suc(x),y) != Add(Mul(x,y),y)`.
The result does not correspond to natural multiplication.

laws.name: Mul base case
laws.equation: Mul(Zero,y) == Zero
laws.falsifier: exhibit y with Mul(Zero,y) != Zero

laws.name: Mul successor recursion
laws.equation: Mul(Suc(x),y) == Add(Mul(x,y),y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y violating the repeated-addition step

laws.name: Mul correctness
laws.equation: UnaryToNat(Mul(x,y)) == UnaryToNat(x) * UnaryToNat(y)
laws.falsifier: exhibit x,y where the Unary product and nat product disagree
